briefs.GPT-1 (Generative Pre-Training):
OpenAI's first GPT, from June 2018, with 117M parameters and a tiny 512-token context. It established the recipe that everything after it runs on: pre-train a Transformer on a pile of unlabeled text, then fine-tune it for specific tasks. The point it proved was that unsupervised pre-training actually transfers — it beat the prior best on 9 of 12 NLP tasks and scored 72.8 on GLUE.

Its strength was conceptual: it showed the path forward and seeded the whole GPT line. By any modern measure it's tiny and weak — a fraction of the size of later models, a context window too short for real documents, and it still needed task-specific fine-tuning to be useful. GPT-2 and GPT-3 surpassed it within two years and made standalone fine-tuning largely unnecessary.
briefs.BERT-Large:
Google's October 2018 encoder model, 340M parameters, that became the workhorse of NLP for the next two years. Unlike the GPT line, BERT reads text bidirectionally — it was trained by masking words and predicting them from both sides — which made it excellent at understanding rather than generating text. It pushed GLUE to 80.5 and posted strong question-answering scores (93.2 F1 on SQuAD v1.1).

It dominated classification, search, and Q&A, and the pre-train/fine-tune pattern it popularized defined the era. Its limits are structural: a 512-token context, and because it's an encoder it can't generate fluent long-form text the way GPT models do. The generative-LLM wave that followed made it feel narrow, though smaller BERT variants still run quietly inside many production systems.
briefs.GPT-2:
OpenAI's February 2019 follow-up, scaled to 1.5B parameters and trained on 40GB of web text. It's famous partly for the rollout: OpenAI staged the release over fears it was 'too dangerous' for misuse, only opening the full model that November. Technically it showed that a big enough language model picks up multitask ability with no task-specific training — zero-shot — and set new marks on 7 of 8 language-modeling datasets.

Its strength was demonstrating that raw scale alone buys general capability, the insight GPT-3 would ride. Limits are obvious in hindsight: a 1024-token context, no instruction-following or chat tuning, and output that drifts off-topic over longer passages. It's a research landmark now, thoroughly outclassed by everything in the GPT-3 era and after.
briefs.Megatron-LM (8.3B):
NVIDIA's September 2019 engineering milestone — an 8.3B-parameter GPT-2-style model whose real contribution was the training method, not the model. It introduced tensor (intra-layer) model parallelism, splitting a single layer across many GPUs, which is what made training dense models past 10B parameters practical. It ran on 512 GPUs at 76% scaling efficiency and set records on WikiText-103, LAMBADA (66.5%), and RACE (90.9%).

Its strength is plumbing: the parallelism techniques here underpin essentially every large model trained since. As an actual language model it's a historical footnote — small by today's standards, text-only, no instruction tuning. The lasting legacy is the systems work, which lived on in later collaborations like the 530B MT-NLG.
briefs.T5-11B (Text-to-Text Transfer Transforme:
Google's October 2019 model, 11B parameters, built on one clean idea: treat every NLP task — translation, summarization, classification, Q&A — as text in, text out. It's an encoder-decoder, pre-trained on the 750GB+ C4 web corpus that Google released alongside it and which is still widely used. The largest variant set new highs on SuperGLUE (88.9), GLUE (90.3), and SQuAD, and the paper was a systematic study of what actually matters in transfer learning.

Its strength was unification and rigor — the text-to-text framing influenced a lot of later design. Limits: a 512-token context, text-only, and no instruction or chat tuning, so it isn't a conversational assistant. Decoder-only models like the GPT line ultimately won the frontier, but T5's framing and the C4 dataset both outlived it.
briefs.GPT-3 (davinci, 175B):
OpenAI's May 2020 model and the anchor of the modern era — 175B parameters, 2048-token context, trained on roughly 300B tokens. Its headline was in-context learning: you could get it to do new tasks just by showing a few examples in the prompt, with no retraining. It hit 86.4% on LAMBADA (an 18-point jump) and 71.2% few-shot on TriviaQA, and it launched the commercial API era — closed weights, pay per call.

Strong at few-shot generalization across a huge range of text tasks, which is what made it feel like a step change. But by current standards it's limited: closed and API-only, a short context, and a then-reported MMLU of just 43.9% few-shot — modest reasoning that later models more than doubled. It also predates instruction tuning, so raw GPT-3 was powerful but awkward to steer compared to the ChatGPT-era models built on top of it.
briefs.OpenAI Codex (code-davinci):
OpenAI's August 2021 code model — GPT-3 (a 12B variant) fine-tuned on public source code, and the first production code-generation LLM. It powered the original GitHub Copilot and introduced HumanEval, the pass/fail coding benchmark that's still a standard reference. On its own benchmark it scored 28.8% pass@1, solving roughly a third of problems on the first try (and 72.3% given 100 attempts).

Its strength was being first and practical: it turned LLMs into a real developer tool and gave the field its canonical coding test. Limits are steep by today's measure — that 28.8% looks low against the 70%+ scores modern models post on the same benchmark, the context was small, and it was closed and API-only. It's been fully superseded, but HumanEval and the Copilot product both came from it.
briefs.Megatron-Turing NLG 530B (MT-NLG):
A Microsoft–NVIDIA collaboration from October 2021, and at the time the largest single dense (non-mixture-of-experts) Transformer ever trained — 530B parameters, 105 layers, built using the DeepSpeed and Megatron stacks across 560 servers of A100 GPUs. It was a statement of what brute-force scaling and serious distributed-training engineering could achieve.

Its significance is mostly as a high-water mark for the 'just make it bigger' approach. The file lists no benchmark scores for it, and that's telling — months later DeepMind's Chinchilla showed that models this size were badly under-trained on data, so a 530B dense model wasn't even compute-optimal. It's closed, text-only, and was quickly eclipsed by smaller, better-trained models. The lasting value is the systems work, not the model.
briefs.Gopher:
DeepMind's December 2021 entry into frontier-scale language models — 280B parameters trained on about 300B tokens — and its first real flagship LM. It came with a broad 152-task evaluation and posted around 60% on MMLU and 54.4 on BIG-bench, establishing DeepMind as a serious player in language AI alongside OpenAI and Google.

Strong as a research baseline, and important for what it enabled next: its compute setup was the reference DeepMind reused to derive the Chinchilla scaling laws. That's also its main limitation in hindsight — Chinchilla showed Gopher was heavily under-trained, and a 70B model trained on far more data beat it at equal compute. Closed, text-only, and quickly outdone by its own lab's follow-up, it reads now as the experiment that set up a bigger insight.
briefs.InstructGPT (text-davinci-002 / GPT-3.5):
OpenAI's January 2022 model, the same 175B GPT-3 scale but trained with RLHF — reinforcement learning from human feedback — to actually follow instructions. This is the alignment breakthrough that made LLMs usable: rather than coaxing GPT-3 with clever prompts, you could just tell InstructGPT what to do. The striking result was that a tiny 1.3B aligned model was preferred by human raters over the full 175B GPT-3, proving alignment can beat raw scale for usefulness.

Its strength is foundational — RLHF and this instruction-following recipe led directly to the GPT-3.5 line and ChatGPT weeks later. It's closed and text-only, and the file lists no benchmark numbers for it; its importance is the technique, not a leaderboard score. Conversationally it was a stepping stone, immediately overshadowed by the chat-tuned ChatGPT built on the same ideas.
briefs.Chinchilla:
DeepMind's Chinchilla (March 2022) is famous less for being a product and more for a finding that redirected the whole field. Its team showed that the giant models of the era were badly under-trained: for a fixed compute budget you should feed roughly 20 tokens of text per parameter, not just pile on more parameters. To prove it, a 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens beat the 280B Gopher, GPT-3, and MT-NLG at equal compute.

That insight ("the Chinchilla scaling laws") moved the industry from "build it bigger" to "train it on more data," and shaped nearly every model that followed. As a model itself it was never publicly released and is now dated: its MMLU of 67.5% was strong for 2022 but is routine for small models today, and its 2K context and text-only scope are long surpassed.
briefs.PaLM (540B):
Google's PaLM (April 2022) was the biggest "dense" language model of its era at 540 billion parameters, trained across two pods of Google's TPU v4 chips (6,144 chips) on the new Pathways system. It set a new top score on MMLU (69.3%) and, more importantly, showed off chain-of-thought prompting and "emergent" abilities, skills that appeared only once a model got large enough.

It was a research demonstration, not a public product, and the pure size-first approach it embodied was quickly undercut: DeepMind's Chinchilla had just argued that smaller, better-trained models win at equal compute, and Google's own PaLM 2 a year later beat it while being smaller. Closed weights, 2K context, and text-only also date it badly against today's multimodal, million-token models.
briefs.BLOOM:
BLOOM (July 2022) was the first genuinely open, fully transparent large language model at GPT-3 scale, 176 billion parameters. It came out of BigScience, a one-year collaboration of roughly 1,000 researchers across 70-plus countries coordinated by Hugging Face, and was built to be multilingual from the start: 46 human languages and 13 programming languages, trained on the open ROOTS corpus (~366B tokens) and shipped under a Responsible AI License.

Its landmark value was openness and process, not raw capability. Even at launch it generally trailed the best closed models, and the file lists no benchmark scores for it. It has since been thoroughly outclassed: later open models like Llama 2 and Falcon matched or beat it at far smaller sizes, and its text-only, modest-context design is well behind today's open releases.
briefs.ChatGPT (GPT-3.5):
ChatGPT (November 30, 2022) is the single biggest public-adoption moment in AI history. It wasn't a new base model so much as a conversational, RLHF-tuned version of OpenAI's GPT-3.5 line (a sibling of InstructGPT) wrapped in a chat interface anyone could use. It hit one million users in five days and roughly 100 million by January 2023, the fastest-growing consumer app at the time, and kicked off the generative-AI mainstream era and the industry-wide LLM race.

Its importance is cultural and historical rather than technical, and the file lists no benchmark numbers for it. The underlying GPT-3.5 was soon eclipsed: GPT-4 arrived months later and far stronger, and the 4K context and text-only scope are now entry-level. "ChatGPT" today refers to a product line built on far newer models than the one that launched here.
briefs.LLaMA (1):
Meta's LLaMA (February 2023) was the open-weights release that lit the fuse on the entire local-LLM movement. Offered in 7B to 65B sizes, it punched far above its weight: the 13B model beat GPT-3's 175B on most benchmarks, and the 65B (MMLU 63.4) rivaled Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B at a fraction of the size. After the weights leaked, it became the base for Alpaca, Vicuna, and a wave of fine-tunes.

Its limits are mostly that the field moved fast past it. The first LLaMA had only a 2K context and was text-only, its license was research-only (not truly commercial), and its successor Llama 2 arrived just five months later with a real commercial license and better numbers. As a capability it's long superseded; its significance is as the spark for open models.
briefs.Claude 1:
Claude 1 (March 14, 2023) was Anthropic's first public assistant, launched the very same day as GPT-4 in two tiers: Claude and the faster, cheaper Claude Instant. It introduced Anthropic's "Constitutional AI" framing, training the model to be helpful, honest, and harmless against a written set of principles, which became the company's signature approach. It started with a roughly 9K-token context, later expanded to 100K with Claude 1.3 in May 2023.

The file does not mark it as a milestone, and it lists no benchmark scores for it. As a first-generation assistant it was quickly overtaken by Anthropic's own rapid cadence, Claude 2 four months later, then the Claude 3 family, and so on, each far more capable. It's of interest now mainly as the origin point of the Claude line.
briefs.GPT-4:
GPT-4 (March 2023) was the model that set the frontier for the rest of the year. It was the first broadly multimodal flagship (accepting images as well as text) and posted scores that defined "frontier" at the time: MMLU 86.4%, HumanEval 67% on coding, and roughly 92% on the GSM8K grade-school math set. Its technical report deliberately withheld size, architecture, and training details (size is only rumored, around 1.8T as a mixture-of-experts), a turning point toward closed frontier development.

Its limits show with age. The default context was just 8K tokens (32K in an extended API variant), small by current standards, and it took images in but couldn't generate them. The benchmarks it once topped are now near-saturated by much cheaper models, and OpenAI's own GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4o, and later lines surpassed it on speed, cost, and capability.
briefs.Falcon 40B:
Falcon 40B (May 2023) came from the UAE's Technology Innovation Institute and was a notable open-weights entry in the post-LLaMA scramble. Trained on a trillion tokens of the carefully filtered RefinedWeb dataset, it topped Hugging Face's Open LLM Leaderboard in mid-2023 and was released under a permissive (later Apache-2.0-style) license for both research and commercial use, which mattered when LLaMA's license was still research-only.

The file doesn't mark it a milestone and lists no benchmark scores, which fits its real status: a strong-for-the-moment open model rather than a paradigm-shifter. It had only a 2K context and was text-only, and it was overtaken quickly, by Llama 2 weeks later and by TII's own Falcon 180B in September. Today it's a historical footnote in the open-model timeline.
briefs.PaLM 2:
PaLM 2 (May 2023) was the engine behind Google's Bard and its broader 2023 AI stack, announced at Google I/O. It shipped in four sizes nicknamed Gecko, Otter, Bison, and Unicorn, and its headline trick was efficiency: it beat the much larger 540B original PaLM while being smaller (reportedly around 340B), with strong multilingual and reasoning skills, MMLU 78.3% and GSM8K 80.7% on math.

It was closed-weights and text-only with an 8K context, and the file doesn't flag it as a milestone, it was a solid flagship rather than a field-mover. It trailed the best of its moment (GPT-4 was already ahead on the hardest benchmarks) and was superseded fast by Google's own Gemini line starting in December 2023, which brought native multimodality and much larger context windows.
briefs.Claude 2:
Claude 2 (July 2023) was Anthropic's long-context breakthrough. Its headline was a 100K-token context window (about 75,000 words), dwarfing GPT-4's 8K/32K at the time and making it the go-to model for reading long documents in 2023. It also brought real capability gains, HumanEval jumped to 71.2% (from Claude 1.3's 56%) and GSM8K math hit 88%, and it launched the first public Claude chat product at claude.ai.

Like its predecessors it's been steadily lapped. Weights and exact size were never disclosed, it was text-only, and the very long-context lead it pioneered became table stakes within a year as rivals shipped 128K, then million-token windows. Anthropic's own Claude 3 family (March 2024) added vision and a 200K context and surpassed it across the board, so Claude 2 now reads as a stepping stone rather than a current option.
briefs.GPT-4 Turbo:
OpenAI shipped this at its first DevDay in November 2023 as a faster, cheaper refresh of GPT-4. The headline was a 128K-token context window — roughly 300 pages in one prompt — which finally matched the long-context bar Claude 2 had set earlier that year. It kept GPT-4's text-plus-image input and pushed its knowledge cutoff forward to April 2023.

Its main job was economics and context length, not raw new intelligence — it was a point release, not a leap, and the file lists no fresh benchmark scores for it. The closed, API-only model has since been fully eclipsed: GPT-4o (2024) matched its smarts at half the cost and double the speed, and the later reasoning and GPT-5 lines left it far behind.
briefs.Gemini 1.0 (Ultra / Pro / Nano):
Google DeepMind's December 2023 answer to GPT-4, and a genuine milestone: the first natively multimodal frontier model, built from the ground up on text, image, audio and video rather than bolting vision onto a text model. The top Ultra tier was the first model to beat the human-expert baseline on MMLU (90.0%) and posted strong GSM8K (94.4), MATH (53.2) and HumanEval (74.4), edging GPT-4 on most of 32 tested benchmarks.

The caveats were real. The flagship Ultra didn't actually ship until early 2024 — only the weaker Pro (MMLU ~71.8) launched in December — and the demo video was criticized as edited. Its 32K context now looks small next to the 1M windows Gemini's own later versions introduced, and its closed weights and benchmark lead have long since been surpassed.
briefs.Mixtral 8x7B:
Mistral AI's December 2023 release was the first strong open sparse Mixture-of-Experts model. It has 8 expert sub-networks but only activates 2 per token, so you get roughly 47B-parameter quality at about 13B's inference cost. Apache-2.0 licensed with a 32K context, it matched or beat Llama 2 70B and GPT-3.5 on most benchmarks (MMLU 70.6) and proved open MoE was viable, kicking off the wider MoE wave.

It was an efficiency and architecture landmark more than a frontier-intelligence one — well below GPT-4-class models even at launch. Text-only, with an MMLU that's modest by today's standards, it's been thoroughly surpassed by later open MoE models like DeepSeek-V3 and the Qwen3 line, which carry the same idea to far larger scale and quality.
briefs.GPT-4o:
OpenAI's May 2024 flagship, the 'o' standing for omni. It was the first model to handle text, audio and vision end-to-end in a single network rather than stitching separate systems together, enabling real-time voice with about 320ms latency. It matched GPT-4 Turbo's intelligence at twice the speed and half the cost, and scored well across the board: MMLU 88.7, HumanEval 90.2, MATH 76.6, GPQA 53.6.

For most of 2024 it was OpenAI's workhorse and a major usability leap, but it's a pre-reasoning model — its GPQA (53.6) and AIME-style math look weak next to the o1 reasoning series that landed months later and the GPT-5 line after that. Closed and API-only, it's since been positioned as a fast, cheaper option rather than the frontier.
briefs.GPT-4o mini:
The budget sibling, released in July 2024 to replace GPT-3.5 Turbo as OpenAI's cheap, fast default. Derived from the omni line, it kept a 128K context and delivered roughly 82% MMLU (plus HumanEval 87.2 and MATH 70.2) at a small fraction of full GPT-4o's price, which made it the go-to API workhorse for high-volume, cost-sensitive jobs.

It was never meant to be smart at the frontier — it's a price-performance play, and on hard reasoning and science it trails the bigger models by a wide margin. Like the rest of the 4o family it predates the reasoning era, so newer cheap tiers (o-series minis, GPT-5 nano/mini, and rival small models) now offer more capability per dollar. Closed weights, text and image only.
briefs.OpenAI o1-preview:
Released September 2024, this is the model that opened the 'reasoning' era. Instead of answering immediately, it spends extra compute thinking through a long internal chain-of-thought, trained via reinforcement learning. The payoff was dramatic on hard problems: AIME competition math jumped from GPT-4o's ~12% to 56.7% solo, alongside GPQA 73.3 and MATH 85.5. It was the first of the o-series and reset how the field thought about scaling.

As a 'preview' it was an early, rough cut — the hidden chain-of-thought wasn't shown to users, it was slower and pricier than standard chat models, and it was tuned for STEM reasoning rather than broad knowledge or writing. The full o1, then o3 and the GPT-5 reasoning line, quickly outscored it. Closed and API-only.
briefs.OpenAI o1-mini:
Launched the same day as o1-preview in September 2024 as the cheap reasoning option — roughly 80% cheaper and specialized for STEM and coding. The surprise was how little it gave up: AIME 70 and MATH 90 put it close to the full o1 on math despite carrying far less general world knowledge. It made inference-time reasoning affordable enough to use at scale.

The trade-off is baked in: it's narrow. Strip away math, code and logic and it has noticeably thinner knowledge than larger models, and its hidden chain-of-thought adds latency and cost versus a plain chat model. It was a transitional small reasoner, since replaced by o3-mini and o4-mini, which push the same niche further. Closed weights, text only.
briefs.OpenAI o1:
OpenAI's first full reasoning model, released December 2024 (with an o1 pro mode) during the "12 Days of OpenAI." It was the production version of the inference-time-compute approach the o1-preview kicked off: the model thinks through a long internal chain of thought before answering, trading speed for much harder problem-solving. Text and image input, 200K context, closed weights.

It was a step-change on reasoning: GPQA 78% (above human PhD-level on that science test), AIME 74.4 on competition math, MATH 94.8, plus roughly 89th-percentile Codeforces coding. The catch is it's slow and pricey because the hidden "thinking" burns extra tokens, the chain of thought is hidden from you, and it's narrowly a reasoning tool. It's since been surpassed by o3 and the GPT-5 line.
briefs.Claude 3 Opus:
Anthropic's flagship of the Claude 3 family, released March 2024. It was the first Claude that credibly matched or beat GPT-4-class models across most benchmarks, and it added vision (image input) plus a 200K-token context window. This was the model that put Anthropic back at the frontier table after the Claude 2 era.

Strong all-rounder for its time: MMLU 86.8, HumanEval 84.9 on coding, MATH 60.1. Weaknesses show with age — GPQA was only 50.4 (science reasoning was still hard pre-"thinking" models), it was the slow, expensive top tier of its family, and weights are closed. It's now far behind: Anthropic's own cheaper Claude 3.5 and later Sonnet/Haiku models surpassed it.
briefs.Claude 3 Sonnet:
The mid-tier, balanced member of Anthropic's March 2024 Claude 3 launch, sitting between the flagship Opus and the budget Haiku. It ran about 2x faster than Opus at lower cost while keeping vision and the same 200K context, aimed at everyday workloads where you don't need the top tier's full horsepower.

It was solid but visibly a step down from Opus: MMLU 79, HumanEval 73, and a weak GPQA of 40.4 on science reasoning. Closed weights, no standout specialty — it was the sensible default, not a leader. It was quickly eclipsed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet just three months later, which beat even Opus, so this version is now purely historical.
briefs.Claude 3 Haiku:
The fastest and cheapest tier of Anthropic's Claude 3 family, released a few days after its siblings in March 2024. The pitch was near-instant responses at the lowest price, while still including vision and the full 200K-token context — a budget option for high-volume or latency-sensitive work.

For a small, cheap model it held up: MMLU 75.2 and HumanEval 75.9 were respectable, beating some larger older models. But it trailed badly on harder reasoning (GPQA just 33.3), and as the entry tier it was never meant for demanding tasks. Closed weights. It's been replaced by Claude 3.5 Haiku and later cheap tiers that are far stronger at the same job.
briefs.Claude 3.5 Sonnet:
Released June 2024, this was the model that redefined price/performance for the year. The notable twist: a mid-tier model that beat its own flagship, Claude 3 Opus, and matched or beat GPT-4o on most benchmarks while running about 2x faster than Opus. It kept vision and 200K context. It showed you didn't need the biggest, priciest tier to lead.

Strong across the board for 2024: MMLU 88.7, HumanEval 92 on coding, MATH 71.1, GPQA 59.4, and an early agentic-coding score of 33.4 on SWE-bench. Limits are mostly age: closed weights, and that SWE-bench number looks low now. Its own October refresh and later Sonnet versions have since passed it.
briefs.Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new / v2):
An upgraded "new" version of Claude 3.5 Sonnet, released October 2024, keeping the same name (which caused some confusion). Its headline was a public beta of "computer use" — letting the model control a graphical interface by looking at the screen and clicking, an early move toward AI agents that operate software like a person.

It jumped SWE-bench Verified to 49.0 on real-world coding tasks, beating OpenAI's o1-preview on agentic coding, with GPQA 65 and MMLU 89. Caveats: computer use was an unreliable beta, weights are closed, and these coding scores have since been blown past — Anthropic's 2025 Sonnet and Opus models sit far higher. It was a frontier point release, not a generational leap.
briefs.Claude 3.5 Haiku:
Anthropic's fast, cheap small model, released November 2024 as the budget tier of the 3.5 generation. The notable claim was that it matched the original Claude 3 Opus — the prior flagship — on many coding tasks, meaning last year's top-tier ability for a fraction of the price. Text-focused, 200K context, closed weights.

Its strength was coding value: SWE-bench Verified 40.6 and HumanEval 88.1 are strong for a small, low-cost model. Limits are inherent to the tier — it's not a deep reasoner, and unlike its 3.5 Sonnet siblings it dropped vision. It's been superseded by later cheap tiers like Claude Haiku 4.5, which deliver near-frontier coding at similar prices.
briefs.Gemini 1.5 Pro:
Google DeepMind's February 2024 model, notable mainly for context length: it was the first mainstream model with a 1-million-token window (2M in preview), meaning it could ingest entire books, codebases, or hours of video at once. It used a Mixture-of-Experts design, was natively multimodal across text, image, audio, and video, and showed near-perfect retrieval across that huge context. GA arrived May 2024.

That long-context-plus-multimodal combo was its real edge, and it tested well: MMLU 85.9, HumanEval 84.1, MATH 67.7. On pure science reasoning it lagged (GPQA 46.2), and weights are closed. It's been surpassed by the Gemini 2.x and 3.x lines, which kept the 1M context while pushing quality much higher.
briefs.Gemini 1.5 Flash:
A distilled, lighter, faster sibling of Gemini 1.5 Pro, announced at Google I/O in May 2024. The point was to keep the headline 1-million-token context and full multimodality (text, image, audio, video) while being cheap and fast enough for high-volume work — a workhorse for processing lots of data rather than a frontier brain.

It traded some quality for that speed and price: MMLU 78.9, HumanEval 74.3, MATH 54.9 — clearly a notch below Pro but fine for bulk tasks. Closed weights, and it was never meant to lead benchmarks. It's been replaced by the Gemini 2.0/3.x Flash line, which offers stronger reasoning at similar speed and cost, so this version is now historical.
briefs.Gemini 2.0 Flash:
The first model of Google's Gemini 2.0 generation, released December 2024 as an experimental build. Despite being a "Flash" (fast/cheap) tier, it ran about 2x faster than Gemini 1.5 Pro while beating it, kept the 1M-token context, and added native tool use, built-in image and audio generation, and an agentic "Multimodal Live" API for real-time interaction.

Its strengths were speed plus newly strong reasoning for the tier: MATH 89.7 and GPQA 65.2 were big jumps over the 1.5 line. The oddity is its MMLU (76.4) actually sits below 1.5 Pro's, so it wasn't uniformly better on knowledge tests. Closed weights, and it was an experimental release. The later Gemini 3.x Flash models have since surpassed it.
briefs.Llama 3 8B:
Meta's small open-weights model from April 2024, part of the Llama 3 launch. Trained on a then-huge 15 trillion tokens, it was built to punch above its 8-billion-parameter weight class and quickly became a go-to base that developers fine-tuned for their own tasks.

For its size it's strong on general knowledge and code (MMLU 66.6, HumanEval 62.2), making it a practical choice to run cheaply or even locally. The limits are real, though: math is weak (MATH 30), the context window is a short 8K tokens, and like any 8B model it trails the larger 70B-plus models on hard reasoning. Newer small models have since passed it.
briefs.Llama 3 70B:
Meta's flagship open model from April 2024 and the one that reasserted Meta's lead in open weights. At 70 billion parameters it closed much of the gap to GPT-4-class systems on general knowledge, giving people a freely downloadable model that was genuinely competitive for the first time in a while.

It's solid across the board: MMLU 79.5, HumanEval 81.7 for coding, MATH 50.4. The main caveat is the cramped 8K-token context window, which limits how much you can feed it at once, and its science reasoning (GPQA 39.5) lags the top closed models. Its own later refreshes (Llama 3.1 and 3.3) made it largely obsolete.
briefs.Llama 3.1 405B:
Meta's giant 405-billion-parameter open model from July 2024 - the first openly available model to genuinely rival the closed frontier of its day, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. The 3.1 update also pushed all the Llama sizes up to a 128K-token context window, a big jump from Llama 3's 8K.

Strong everywhere: MMLU 88.6, HumanEval 89, MATH 73.8, GPQA 51.1. The catch is sheer size - 405 billion dense parameters makes it expensive and hardware-hungry to actually run, which is why most people reached for the smaller 70B instead. It has since been overtaken by cheaper mixture-of-experts open models like DeepSeek-V3.
briefs.Llama 3.1 70B:
The July 2024 refresh of Llama 3 70B - same 70-billion-parameter size, but with the context window stretched from 8K to 128K tokens and across-the-board quality gains. It was the practical sweet spot of the Llama 3.1 lineup: most of the big model's smarts without the giant model's cost.

A strong open mid-size workhorse, scoring MMLU 86, MATH 68, HumanEval 80.5, GPQA 46.7 - a clear step up from the original 70B. It's not frontier-leading and doesn't top any single benchmark; it trails the 405B sibling and the best closed models. It was effectively superseded a few months later by Llama 3.3 70B, which matched it and then some.
briefs.Llama 3.3 70B:
Meta quietly dropped this on Hugging Face in December 2024 with no big launch. The headline trick: it delivered close to 405B-level quality at the much smaller 70B size and cost, beating the older Claude 3 Opus on five of six major benchmarks - a sign of how fast distillation and training know-how were compressing capability into smaller models.

Strong all-rounder with a 128K context: MMLU 86, MATH 77, HumanEval 88.4, GPQA 50.5. Its Artificial Analysis Index score of 14 places it well below the reasoning-era frontier that arrived right around the same time, and it's a text-only model with no vision or built-in reasoning mode. Useful and cheap, but no longer near the top.
briefs.DeepSeek-V2:
A May 2024 open model from the Chinese lab DeepSeek, and an efficiency milestone. It's a mixture-of-experts design - 236 billion total parameters but only 21 billion active per token - and it introduced Multi-head Latent Attention, a memory trick that made inference radically cheaper. Its low pricing helped kick off China's LLM price war.

Good, not frontier: MMLU 78.5, HumanEval 81.1, with weaker math at MATH 43.6. The real story is cost-per-token rather than raw intelligence, and on quality it sat behind the top closed models of mid-2024. Its much stronger successor, DeepSeek-V3, arrived seven months later and made it the stepping stone rather than the destination.
briefs.DeepSeek-V3:
DeepSeek's December 2024 open model and the one that genuinely rattled the industry. A 671-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (37B active), it reportedly cost only about $5.6 million to train using FP8 precision and their latent-attention method - a fraction of what rivals spent - yet matched GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Open weights made that doubly striking.

Strong across the board: MMLU 88.5, MATH 90.2, GPQA 59.1, HumanEval 82.6. It's a standard (non-reasoning) chat model, so it predates the chain-of-thought reasoning push that its own sibling DeepSeek-R1 would lead a month later, and later versions (V3.1) folded reasoning in. As released it's text-only, with no vision.
briefs.Qwen2-72B:
Alibaba's open 72-billion-parameter model from June 2024, with a 128K-token context and broad multilingual coverage. It topped open-model leaderboards in the middle of that year and reinforced that Chinese labs were now shipping serious, freely downloadable competitors to Meta's Llama line.

Strong on general knowledge (MMLU 84.2) and respectable on math (MATH 59.7), but coding was a relative weak point (HumanEval 64.6) and science reasoning lagged (GPQA 37.9). It's a dense text-only model with no vision or reasoning mode. Alibaba's own Qwen2.5-72B replaced it just three months later with big jumps in math and code, so its time at the top was brief.
briefs.Qwen2.5-72B:
The September 2024 flagship of Alibaba's sprawling Qwen2.5 family, which spanned tiny 0.5B models up to 72B plus dedicated Coder and Math variants. Trained on 18 trillion tokens, it became the leading open base that the community fine-tuned on top of, much as Llama had been earlier.

The standout gain over Qwen2 was math, jumping from MATH 69 to 83.1, alongside MMLU 86.1 and HumanEval 86.6 for coding. Science reasoning (GPQA 49) still trailed the best closed models, and it's a dense text-only model without a built-in reasoning mode or vision. It was a strong open option for late 2024, since surpassed by the Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 generations.
briefs.Mistral Large:
French lab Mistral AI's first closed, commercial flagship, from February 2024. It launched alongside a Microsoft Azure partnership and the 'Le Chat' assistant, and at release ranked second only to GPT-4 on the MMLU knowledge benchmark - a strong showing for a young European challenger.

Good on general knowledge (MMLU 81.2) but noticeably weak on coding (HumanEval 45.1) and middling on math (MATH 45), with a relatively short 32K-token context. Unlike most of Mistral's reputation-making releases, this one was closed-weight. Its open successor, Mistral Large 2, landed five months later with far better code and a 128K context, making this first version mostly a historical marker.
briefs.Mistral Large 2:
Mistral AI's 123B dense model, out July 2024 with a 128K-token context. Unlike the closed first-gen Mistral Large, this one shipped with open weights (under a research, non-commercial license), making it a rare frontier-adjacent model you could actually download. It was pitched as matching Llama 3.1 405B while being roughly a third the size.

Its strengths are code and math: HumanEval 92 and MATH 71.5 are genuinely strong, with solid multilingual coverage and MMLU 84. The catches: the license blocks commercial use without a separate deal, and on broad knowledge (MMLU 84, GPQA 48) it trails the true frontier of its day. A point release in a fast-moving line, now well behind 2025-2026 models.
briefs.OpenAI o3-mini:
A small 'reasoning' model from OpenAI, released January 2025 with a 200K context. It's part of the o-series that thinks step-by-step before answering, tuned here for cheap STEM problem-solving — roughly o1-level reasoning at medium effort for a fraction of the cost. Text-only.

Where it shines is math and science: AIME (2024) 87.3 and GPQA Diamond 79.7 at high effort are excellent for a budget model. The trade-offs are inherent to the small-and-cheap design — less world knowledge than the full-size models, no image input, and it's been superseded by o3 and o4-mini, which push the same benchmarks higher. Closed weights, API-only.
briefs.DeepSeek-R1:
The open-weights reasoning shock of January 2025, from Chinese lab DeepSeek. A 671B Mixture-of-Experts model (only 37B active per token), it was the first openly released model to rival OpenAI's o1 on math and science, trained heavily with reinforcement learning and shipped under a permissive MIT license with a public technical report. Its arrival triggered a market-wide selloff.

Strengths are reasoning: AIME (2024) 79.8 and GPQA 71.5, all in weights anyone can run or fine-tune. Caveats: as a reasoning model it's text-only and burns tokens 'thinking,' the 671B size demands serious hardware, and a May 2025 refresh (R1-0528) already pushed those numbers well past the original. A landmark, now an older checkpoint.
briefs.GPT-4.5 (Orion):
OpenAI's GPT-4.5, codenamed Orion, landed Feb 2025 as the company's largest model trained purely by scaling up pretraining rather than the new reasoning approach. It was a closed, text-and-vision chat model with a 128K context, deliberately positioned for emotional intelligence, writing quality, and lower hallucination rather than step-by-step problem solving.

Its strength was conversational feel and reduced making-things-up, not benchmark dominance; the file lists no benchmark scores for it. Its weakness was that the pure-scaling bet had hit diminishing returns just as reasoning models took over. It was deprecated from the API July 14 2025 in favor of GPT-4.1, effectively marking the end of OpenAI's just-make-it-bigger era.
briefs.Claude 3.7 Sonnet:
Anthropic's Claude 3.7 Sonnet, out Feb 2025, was its first hybrid reasoning model: you could toggle extended thinking on or off in one model. It shipped alongside Claude Code, the coding agent, with a 200K context and a 128K-token output ceiling in thinking mode, and it set the template for the agentic-coding wave that followed.

Its standout strength was software engineering: it scored about 70.3% on SWE-bench Verified (with custom scaffolding), near the top at launch. It's text-plus-vision only, with no image or audio output, and its single listed benchmark is coding-focused. By mid-2026 it has been clearly surpassed by Anthropic's own Sonnet 4.x and Opus 4.x line, which push SWE-bench well into the high 80s.
briefs.xAI Grok 3:
xAI's Grok 3, released Feb 2025, was trained on the company's Colossus supercomputer, reportedly a 100,000-to-200,000-GPU cluster. It's a closed text-and-vision model with a 128K context that added a 'Think' reasoning mode and a DeepSearch web agent, marking xAI's serious push into frontier reasoning.

It posted strong math and science numbers using heavy test-time compute (consensus over 64 samples): 84.6% on GPQA Diamond and 93.3% on AIME 2025. The caveat is that those top figures lean on that extra compute rather than a single pass, and the weights are closed. It has since been overtaken by xAI's own Grok 4 and later Grok 4.x releases, which roughly 100x its training compute.
briefs.Google Gemini 2.5 Pro:
Google DeepMind's Gemini 2.5 Pro, out March 2025, was a native 'thinking' model with a huge 1M-token context and full multimodal input across text, image, audio, and video. At launch it topped the LMArena human-preference leaderboard and led several math and science benchmarks.

Strengths: broad reasoning and a then-record 18.8% on Humanity's Last Exam without tools, plus 84% GPQA and 86.7% on AIME 2025. The HLE score, impressive at the time, looks modest now: by late 2025 and into 2026, models like Gemini 3 Pro and Claude Opus 4.8 push HLE far higher. It's closed-weight and API/app-only, and has been superseded within Google's own lineup by the Gemini 3.x family.
briefs.Meta Llama 4 Scout:
Meta's Llama 4 Scout, released April 2025, was the first natively-multimodal mixture-of-experts Llama, with 109B total parameters but only 17B active per token across 16 experts. Its headline feature was a 10M-token context window, the largest of any open model at launch, and it handles both text and image input.

Its strength is that enormous context plus efficient open-weight deployment: you get a big model's reach at a 17B-active compute cost. The file lists no benchmark scores for it, so raw capability claims stay general, and it's open-weight but under Meta's Llama 4 community license, not a true OSI-approved open license. In practice the gigantic context was more a spec milestone than a guarantee of strong recall throughout that whole window.
briefs.Meta Llama 4 Maverick:
Meta's Llama 4 Maverick, also April 2025, is the larger sibling to Scout: 400B total parameters with 17B active across 128 experts, a natively-multimodal text-and-image MoE with a 1M-token context. It was distilled from a roughly 288B-active 'Behemoth' teacher model and pitched as beating GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash while rivaling DeepSeek V3 on reasoning and coding.

Its appeal is frontier-adjacent quality at far fewer active parameters, with open weights under the Llama 4 community license. The catches: the file lists no benchmark scores, so those comparison claims are Meta's framing rather than verified numbers here, and the flagship Behemoth teacher it was distilled from never actually shipped in 2025. It's open-weight but not OSI-open, and has since been outpaced by newer open models.
briefs.OpenAI o3:
OpenAI's April 2025 reasoning flagship and the first of its models to use tools — web search, Python, image analysis — inside its own chain of thought. That made it the template for 'agentic reasoning,' where the model acts during thinking rather than just answering. Text-plus-vision input, 200K context.

The benchmarks are top-tier: GPQA 87.7, SWE-bench Verified 71.7, and AIME (2025) 98.4 with tools, plus a Codeforces rating around 2727 Elo that puts it near competitive-programmer level. Caveats: that near-perfect AIME leans on tool use, reasoning models are slower and pricier per task, and o4-mini and the GPT-5 line have since pushed past it. Closed weights, API-only. A genuine milestone in how these models work.
briefs.OpenAI o4-mini:
A small, cheap reasoning model from OpenAI, released April 2025 alongside the bigger o3 as the first entry in the "o4" line. Like the rest of the o-series, it thinks before answering and can use tools (web, vision, and notably a Python interpreter) mid-reasoning. It has a 200K-token context and handles text plus image input.

Its standout is math: it posts a near-perfect 99.5% on AIME 2025 when allowed to run a Python interpreter, basically best-in-class for a budget model. The caveat is that the headline number leans on that tool, and as a deliberately small/cheap reasoner it carries less raw world knowledge than full-size flagships. The file lists no other benchmarks for it, so its strength outside of math/coding is less documented here.
briefs.Alibaba Qwen3-235B-A22B:
Alibaba's open-weights flagship from the Qwen3 family, released April 2025 under the permissive Apache-2.0 license. It's a Mixture-of-Experts model: 235B total parameters but only 22B active per token, which keeps inference cheaper than its size suggests. Its signature trick is a single-model "thinking / non-thinking" toggle, so you switch reasoning on or off without swapping models. Context is 128K.

Its strength is being a leading open release of 2025 that's pitched as competitive with closed and semi-closed reasoners like DeepSeek-R1, o1, Grok 3, and Gemini 2.5 Pro, all while you can download and run the weights yourself. The catch: the file lists no benchmark numbers for it, so those competitive claims are positioning rather than scores you can check here, and like all open models it depends on you having the hardware to serve it.
briefs.Claude Opus 4:
Anthropic's frontier flagship, released May 2025, built specifically for long-horizon autonomous work, the kind of multi-step coding and agent tasks that Claude Code runs in the background. It's a hybrid model that can answer instantly or switch into extended reasoning, with a 200K context and text-plus-vision input.

Its strength is agentic coding: it led the field at launch with about 72.5% on SWE-bench Verified (real software-engineering tasks), plus 79.6% GPQA and 75.5% AIME with extended thinking. The limitation is mostly that it has since been clearly surpassed within Anthropic's own line, the later 4.6/4.7/4.8 Opus models push SWE-bench into the high 80s, so by mid-2026 Opus 4 reads as the model that opened the agentic-coding era rather than the one leading it.
briefs.Claude Sonnet 4:
The mid-tier, cost-efficient companion to Claude Opus 4, released the same day in May 2025 as the successor to Claude 3.7 Sonnet. Same hybrid reasoning design (instant or extended thinking), same 200K context, text-plus-vision input, but priced and positioned as the everyday workhorse rather than the top flagship.

What's notable is that it nearly matches its own flagship on coding: about 72.7% on SWE-bench Verified, essentially tied with Opus 4, plus 75.4% GPQA, at lower cost. The limitation is breadth, the file lists fewer benchmarks for it (no AIME, for instance), and as the cheaper tier it's tuned for strong general/coding work rather than topping the hardest reasoning tests. It has also since been superseded by the Sonnet 4.5/4.6 generation.
briefs.DeepSeek-R1-0528:
A major mid-2025 refresh of DeepSeek's open-weights reasoning model R1, released May 2025 under the permissive MIT license. Same architecture as the original, a 671B Mixture-of-Experts with only 37B active per token, 128K context, text-only, focused on chain-of-thought reasoning.

The upgrade was substantial: AIME 2025 jumped from 70.0 to 87.5 and GPQA from 71.5 to 81.0, with fewer hallucinations and new JSON and function-calling support, bringing the leading open model back in line with Google and OpenAI's reasoners. The caveats are practical, it's a big model to host even with sparse activation, it's text-only with no vision, and these are very strong but not chart-topping scores against the absolute frontier of the period.
briefs.xAI Grok 4:
xAI's frontier model, released July 2025, trained on the 200,000-GPU Colossus cluster with roughly 100x the compute of Grok 2. It's a reported ~1.7T-parameter MoE with a 256K context and text-plus-vision input, built around native tool-use reasoning, the model calls tools inside its chain of thought. It briefly led the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at launch.

It's strong on hard reasoning: 87.7% GPQA, around 94.3% on AIME 2025, and 23.9% on Humanity's Last Exam, with a multi-agent "Grok 4 Heavy" variant pushing HLE to ~44% using tools. The caveats are that the biggest numbers depend on heavy test-time compute and the multi-agent setup, the parameter count is reported rather than confirmed, the weights are closed, and its index lead was short-lived as GPT-5 and Gemini 3 followed.
briefs.GPT-5:
OpenAI's August 2025 flagship and a structural shift: instead of one model, it's a unified system with an automatic router that decides between a fast model and a slower "thinking" reasoning model per query. It ships in several sizes (gpt-5, mini, nano, pro), has a 400K total context (272K input), and is multimodal on text and vision. It was the frontier leader on the AA Intelligence Index at launch.

Strengths span coding and reasoning: about 74.9% on SWE-bench Verified, 88.4% GPQA, 94.6% AIME, and ~42% on Humanity's Last Exam (that HLE figure is GPT-5 Pro with tools). The caveats are that the top numbers come from the most expensive Pro tier with tool access, and its reign was brief, by early 2026 Gemini 3 and OpenAI's own GPT-5.x line had matched or passed it.
briefs.DeepSeek-V3.1:
An August 2025 open-weights release from DeepSeek that fuses two of its earlier models into one, the direct-answering V3 and the chain-of-thought R1, so a single model can run in thinking or non-thinking mode via the chat template. It keeps the 671B-total / 37B-active MoE design and 128K context, text-only, and is a step toward DeepSeek's unified agentic line.

Its appeal is open weights plus the convenience of one hybrid model instead of two, useful if you want to self-host both fast and reasoning behavior. The honest caveat: the file lists no benchmark numbers for it at all, so there's nothing here to quantify how it stacks up. As an incremental fusion release (not flagged as a milestone) it reads as a consolidation step rather than a capability leap, and it remains text-only.
briefs.GPT-5.1:
A November 2025 refresh of GPT-5 rather than a new generation. It keeps the same 400K context and the router-plus-reasoning architecture, and ships as two flavors: GPT-5.1 Instant and GPT-5.1 Thinking. The headline changes are about feel, not raw capability, a "warmer" default personality and eight selectable personalities. The API arrived a day after launch, with more variants following on Nov 19.

Its strength is being a smoother, more steerable version of an already-frontier system, with the personality controls as the main user-facing addition. The limitation is that it's explicitly a point release, not flagged as a milestone, and the file lists no benchmarks for it, so there's no measured capability jump to point to here. Weights are closed, and within months OpenAI's own GPT-5.3/5.4/5.5 line moved past it.
briefs.Google Gemini 3 Pro:
Google DeepMind's frontier model, released November 2025 and described as the last major frontier launch of that year. It's a natively "thinking" model that's fully multimodal across text, image, audio, and video, with a 1M-token context. At release it set records on the hardest evals of the period.

Its strengths are top-end reasoning and science: 91.9% on GPQA Diamond and a then-record 37.5% on Humanity's Last Exam with no tools, with a "Deep Think" mode pushing those to 93.8% and 41.0%. The caveats: the very highest figures require the slower Deep Think mode, the weights are closed, and the lead didn't hold for long, the 2026 wave (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Google's own Gemini 3.1 Pro) moved the frontier past these numbers within a few months.
briefs.GPT-5.3-Codex:
OpenAI's specialized coding model, released February 2026. It's a Codex-line flagship — purpose-built for agentic coding (writing and editing code across a whole project, running tools) rather than general chat. Roughly 25% faster than the model it replaced, with a 192K-token context. A lighter "Spark" variant shipped with a smaller 128K window. The coding gains it produced were later folded into OpenAI's general GPT-5.4.

Its strength is narrow and deep: agentic software work, where it scores 56.8 on SWE-bench Pro (a hard real-world coding test). The flip side is exactly that narrowness — it's a coding tool, not a general reasoner, and it takes text and images in but only outputs text. Closed weights, and no public pricing was listed. By the time GPT-5.4 absorbed its coding ability, this point-release was more a stepping stone than a destination.
briefs.GPT-5.4:
OpenAI's general flagship from March 2026. It folded the GPT-5.3-Codex coding engine into a broad multimodal reasoner (text and image in, text out) with a 1M-token context window. Priced at $2.50 per million input tokens and $15 output, with a pricier Pro tier at $30/$180. Mini and nano versions followed two weeks later.

Strong all-rounder: GPQA 92.8 (PhD-level science questions) and SWE-bench Pro 57.7 put it near the top of its cluster. Its notable weakness is symbolic — it was the first new OpenAI flagship that did NOT outright top the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, only tying Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro at 57. So it's frontier-class but no longer the lone leader, a sign of how tight the race had gotten. Closed weights.
briefs.GPT-5.5:
OpenAI's April 2026 flagship, which briefly led the field at an Artificial Analysis Index of roughly 60.2 before Anthropic's Opus 4.8 edged it out at 61.4. It shipped in Thinking, Pro, and Instant variants plus a security-focused GPT-5.5-Cyber model. Multimodal in, text out, with a 1M-token context.

Genuinely strong on hard agentic and math work: 82.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, and 51.7/35.4 on the FrontierMath tiers (some of the toughest math benchmarks going). The catch is cost — per-token price doubled to $5 input / $30 output versus the prior generation, a steep jump. Its top spot was also short-lived, overtaken within weeks. Note the listed GPQA of 0 is a missing value, not a real score. Closed weights.
briefs.GPT-5.5 Pro:
The premium, deep-reasoning tier of OpenAI's GPT-5.5, released April 2026. It's the heavyweight variant aimed at agentic and research-grade work — long autonomous reasoning chains, harder problems — with extra API safeguards and no free tier. Multimodal in, text out, 1M-token context.

Its strength is raw capability headroom for the most demanding tasks, but the defining trait here is price: at $30 per million input tokens and $180 output, it was the most expensive OpenAI tier of the cycle, many times the cost of the standard GPT-5.5. No separate benchmark figures are listed for it in the data, so its scores aren't broken out independently. Closed weights, and overkill for anything routine — you pay that premium only when the task genuinely needs it.
briefs.Claude Opus 4.6:
Anthropic's flagship from February 2026 and the first Opus with a 1M-token context window (in beta), alongside 128K-token output. It introduced "adaptive thinking" and "agent teams" in Claude Code — letting the model spin up coordinated sub-agents for bigger jobs. Multimodal in, text out. Priced at $5 input / $25 output per million tokens.

A strong coding and reasoning model: 80.8 on SWE-bench, 91.3 on GPQA, and 51.9 on the harder SWE-bench Pro. Its limitation is mostly that it was an interim step — its Artificial Analysis Index of 53 sat below the later Opus 4.7 (57.3) and 4.8 (61.4) that followed within months, so it was quickly surpassed inside its own family. Closed weights.
briefs.Claude Sonnet 4.6:
Anthropic's mid-tier workhorse from February 2026 — the balanced, cheaper sibling to Opus 4.6. Multimodal in, text out, with a 1M-token beta context and 64K output. At $3 input / $15 output per million tokens, it's meaningfully cheaper than Opus while landing within a point or two of it on coding.

The value story is the strength: SWE-bench 79.6 (just behind Opus 4.6), a 4.3x jump on the abstract-reasoning ARC-AGI-2 test versus the prior Sonnet (58.3), plus solid Terminal-Bench 2.0 (59.1) and computer-use OSWorld (72.5). Blind users actually preferred it to the older Opus 4.5 about 59% of the time. The trade-off is the usual mid-tier one: on the very hardest problems the full Opus line still pulls ahead. Closed weights.
briefs.Claude Opus 4.7:
Anthropic's flagship from April 2026, a point release that made a big leap on the hardest coding tasks. It added an "xhigh" effort level for tougher problems, higher-resolution vision (up to 2576px), and file-system memory recall so it can pull back relevant context on its own. Multimodal in, text out, 1M-token beta context. Priced at $5/$25 per million tokens.

Genuinely frontier on coding and science: SWE-bench 87.6, SWE-bench Pro 64.3, GPQA 94.2 — all jumps over Opus 4.6. Its main caveat is that the very next release outclassed it: its Artificial Analysis Index of 57.3 sat 4.1 points below Opus 4.8. There's also a documented quirk in this generation — a tendency toward agreeable, sycophantic responses in conversational work — that 4.8 specifically set out to fix. Closed weights.
briefs.Claude Opus 4.8:
Anthropic's late-May 2026 flagship and, at the time, the most capable model in the file. It retook the #1 spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 61.4, beating OpenAI's GPT-5.5 (60.2), and led Humanity's Last Exam at 57.9 (with tools) — a brutal expert-level test. Multimodal in, text out, 1M-token beta context, $5/$25 per million tokens. It added a "Dynamic Workflows" preview.

Top-tier across the board: SWE-bench 88.6, SWE-bench Pro 69.2, GPQA 93.6, and 84% on the Online-Mind2Web agent benchmark. Anthropic reports it's about 4x less likely than Opus 4.7 to let a flaw slip through. The honest caveat: it's a closed-weights, premium-priced frontier model, and within roughly two weeks the (later-pulled) Fable 5 posted higher raw coding numbers — the lead at this tier is measured in weeks, not months.
briefs.Claude Haiku 4.5:
Anthropic's small, fast, cheap tier. It actually shipped in October 2025 — before this tracker's main Feb-Jun 2026 window — but remained the current small-tier Claude through mid-2026, which is why it's here. Multimodal in, text out, with a 200K context and 64K output. Priced at just $1 input / $5 output per million tokens.

The appeal is near-frontier coding at budget cost: 73.3 on SWE-bench is remarkable for a model this cheap, making it the go-to engine for multi-agent setups where you run many calls and care about price. Its limits are the expected small-model ones — it trails the Opus and Sonnet tiers on the harder tests (SWE-bench Pro 39.5, OSWorld 50.7), so it's the efficient workhorse, not the model you reach for on the toughest problems. Closed weights.
briefs.Claude Fable 5:
Claude Fable 5 is Anthropic's Mythos-class flagship, the model with the highest reported SWE-bench Verified score of the cycle (~95%). It was briefly withdrawn worldwide by a US export-control order in June 2026, then cleared and reinstated July 1. As of this sweep it sits #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 60 (v4.1), ahead of its own Opus 4.8 (56) and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 (55).

Its strength is raw frontier intelligence and agentic coding — Anthropic is now 'nearly 5 points ahead of any other lab's best model' on the composite index. The tradeoff is cost: at $10/$50 per million tokens it is the most expensive tier in Anthropic's lineup, aimed at the hardest reasoning and long-horizon coding work rather than high-volume use, where Sonnet 5 or Haiku are the economical picks.
briefs.Mistral Large 3:
Mistral AI's open-weight flagship. Like Haiku 4.5, it predates this tracker's main window (released December 2025) but stayed Mistral's active flagship through 2026. It's a large 675B-total / 41B-active sparse mixture-of-experts model with a 256K context, released under the permissive Apache 2.0 license. Small Ministral 3 siblings (3B/8B/14B) shipped alongside it.

Two real strengths: it's open-weight — you can download and self-host it, unlike the closed OpenAI/Anthropic/Google flagships — and it's very cheap at $0.50 input / $1.50 output per million. It posts a strong MATH-500 of 93.6 and MMLU-Pro of 80.7. The weakness is at the top end: its GPQA of 68 trails the 90-plus scores of the leading 2026 closed frontier models, so it's a cost-effective open option rather than a benchmark leader.
briefs.Llama 2:
Meta's July 2023 open-weights release (7B/13B/70B), and the first frontier-adjacent open model with a genuine commercial license — which made it the default open base layer the whole ecosystem built on for the next year. It came in pretrained and RLHF chat variants, trained on 40% more data than the original LLaMA, with a 4K context. The 70B scored MMLU 68.9, GSM8K 56.8, HumanEval 29.9.

For its moment it was the open model to beat, especially for fine-tuning. By today's standards it's badly dated: 4K context is tiny, and that ~30% HumanEval coding score is a fraction of what 2026 models post (often 80–95%). Newer open families — Llama 3.x, Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM — have surpassed it on every axis, so it's now historical foundation rather than a tool you'd reach for.
briefs.Falcon 180B:
From the UAE's Technology Innovation Institute, released September 2023. Its claim to fame was scale: at 180B parameters trained on 3.5T tokens, it was the largest openly-released LLM at the time. It scored MMLU ~68.7, edging out Llama 2 on that benchmark and approaching Google's PaLM 2. It shipped under the Falcon-180B license (Apache-2.0-based, with some use restrictions).

It was a 'bigger is better' open flagship, useful for showing a non-US lab could play at frontier scale. But it was never very efficient — 180B params for roughly Llama-2-70B-level quality — and its 2K context is tiny by modern standards. The field quickly moved to Mixture-of-Experts designs (DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM) that deliver far more capability per unit of compute, leaving dense giants like this one behind.
briefs.Mistral 7B:
Mistral AI's September 2023 debut model, and an efficiency landmark. At just 7.3B parameters under a clean Apache-2.0 license, it beat the much larger Llama 2 13B on every benchmark and rivaled 34B-class models on reasoning. It introduced grouped-query and sliding-window attention (8K context via a 4K sliding window) and became one of the most-downloaded fine-tuning bases of its era.

Its strength was punching far above its size — a genuinely capable model that ran on modest hardware. The flip side is that it's small and old: no benchmark scores are even logged for it here, its context is short by current norms, and it has no multimodal or reasoning features. Later small models (Llama 3 8B, Qwen, and Mistral's own Ministral line) have since surpassed it while keeping the same efficiency pitch.
briefs.Claude Mythos 5 (Preview):
Claude Mythos 5 is Anthropic's strongest cybersecurity-focused model, the enterprise sibling of the consumer Fable 5. Both were pulled worldwide on Jun 12 2026 by a US Commerce export-control order after researchers showed their guardrails could be bypassed. On Jun 26 2026 the government partially reversed course: a letter from Commerce Secretary Lutnick cleared Mythos 5 for roughly 100 trusted US institutions — agencies and companies that operate and defend critical infrastructure, plus their non-US staff.

Its strength is offensive/defensive security work: in a Congressional demo it found and then patched a simulated banking vulnerability, and it reportedly surfaced flaws in classified US systems — the very capability that triggered the freeze. The limits are access, not ability: it remains export-controlled for everyone outside the approved list, its benchmark figures are preview-grade rather than independently verified, and there's no timeline for broad availability or for restoring the consumer Fable 5 version.
briefs.Gemini 3.1 Pro:
Google DeepMind's frontier flagship from February 19 2026. At launch it took the top spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (57), a full two weeks before OpenAI's GPT-5.4 managed only to tie it. It's natively multimodal — including native video input — with a 1M-token context (64K output). Benchmarks: GPQA 94.3 (the highest in its peer cluster), SWE-bench 80.6, and HLE 51.4.

Its strengths are broad: best-in-cluster science reasoning (GPQA), huge context, and full multimodality including video. Where it's not the outright leader is coding — its 80.6 SWE-bench trails the top Claude models of the period (Opus 4.7/4.8 in the high 80s) — and it later shared the No. 1 Index slot rather than holding it alone. No public per-token price is listed here. It's closed-weights, API/product only.
briefs.Gemini 3 Flash:
Google DeepMind's fast, cheap tier in the Gemini 3 line (2026). The pitch is Pro-grade reasoning at Flash speed and cost: it's multimodal (text, image, speech, video in; text out) with a 1M-token context, priced very low at $0.50 in / $3 out per million tokens. Its non-reasoning AA Index score is 35.

It's built for high-volume, latency-sensitive work where cost matters more than topping a leaderboard — that AA Index of 35 is well below frontier flagships (which sit in the 50s–60s), so it's a workhorse, not a reasoning champion. The line iterated quickly: Gemini 3.5 Flash (AA 50, May 2026) and a 3.1 Flash-Lite (AA 25) followed, so this exact version was already being superseded within its own family. Closed weights.
briefs.DiffusionGemma:
A June 10 2026 release from Google DeepMind, and a genuine architectural first: the first open-weight text-DIFFUSION LLM. Instead of generating tokens one at a time (autoregression, how nearly every other model here works), it denoises 256-token blocks in parallel. It's a 25.2B-total / ~3.8B-active MoE, open under Apache 2.0, with day-zero support across vLLM, Hugging Face, MLX and SGLang.

Its headline strength is raw speed — over 1000 tokens/second on a single H100, up to 4x faster than comparable models — plus being fully open. The explicit tradeoff is quality: it deliberately sits below Gemma 4, so you're buying throughput at the cost of some accuracy. It's also a research-forward oddity rather than a general daily driver: no standard benchmark scores are logged here, and its context length isn't even specified.
briefs.Grok 4.20 Beta:
An xAI beta line from March 2026, framed as a rapid-iteration testbed rather than a finished flagship. 'Beta 2' (March 3) fixed a grab-bag of issues — instruction-following, hallucinations, LaTeX rendering, image search — and a later reasoning variant (0309 v2, April 7) scored 49 on the AA Index. It's multimodal in, text out.

The value here was watching xAI patch and improve in public, fast. But it was explicitly a beta: the 49 AA Index puts it solidly mid-pack, below the frontier cluster in the 53–61 range, and much of its detail (params, context, price) is simply unlisted. It was a stepping stone to the more polished Grok 4.3, not a model you'd choose on the merits over its successors.
briefs.Grok 4.3:
xAI's May 2026 'cheap frontier' play (beta April 17, public API April 30, GA early May). It's multimodal with native video input and a 1M-token context, and it's priced aggressively at $1.25 in / $2.50 out per million tokens. Its AA Index score is 53.

The whole pitch is value: you get near-frontier capability, video, and a million-token window for a fraction of what the top closed models charge. The honest limitation is that it's not actually at the top — its 53 AA Index sits below GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro (both ~57) and well under Opus 4.8 (61.4). So it's the budget-conscious choice when you want a lot of capability and long context per dollar, not when you need the single sharpest model available.
briefs.Ministral 3:
Mistral AI's small/edge model line from December 2025, paired with the larger Mistral Large 3 flagship. It comes in 3B, 8B and 14B variants with an unusually large 256K context for its size, open weights, and is GA on Amazon Bedrock. Mistral markets it as best-in-class performance-per-cost for small models.

Its strength is exactly that: cheap, deployable models you can run at the edge or in volume, with a long context window. The flip side is that no benchmark scores are logged for it here, so its quality claims rest on Mistral's own positioning rather than independent numbers in this dataset — and as a small-model line it's not competing on raw intelligence with the frontier MoE giants, just on efficiency and footprint.
briefs.Qwen3.5-397B-A17B:
Alibaba's Qwen3.5 flagship, released February 16 2026. It's a 397B-total / 17B-active Mixture-of-Experts model (512 experts) and the first Qwen open model with native vision, supporting 201 languages with a 256K context. At launch it was the #3 open-weights model on the AA Index (45). Benchmarks: SWE-bench 76.4, GPQA 88.4, MMLU-Pro 87.8, AIME 2026 91.3.

Strengths: it's open-weight, natively multimodal, broadly multilingual, and notably efficient — Alibaba reports an 8.6–19x throughput gain, with its 256K context decoding ~19x faster than the older Qwen3-Max, while beating Alibaba's own trillion-parameter model at lower cost. The caveat is the ceiling: an AA Index of 45 is solid for open weights but clearly below the closed frontier (mid-50s and up), so it's a strong open option rather than an outright leader.
briefs.Kimi K2.7 Code:
Moonshot AI's June 12 2026 open-weight coding model (Modified MIT license). It's a huge 1T-total / 32B-active MoE (384 experts) with a 256K context, built coding-first for agentic work, and tuned for efficiency — about 30% fewer reasoning tokens than the prior K2.6. Priced at $0.95 in / $4.00 out per million tokens.

The real strength is being a frontier-scale open coding model you can actually run and modify. The major caveat is verification: every performance number Moonshot published is from its OWN proprietary benchmarks (e.g. Kimi Code Bench v2, +21.8%), with NO independent SWE-bench, GPQA, or Terminal-Bench results available as of release. So its quality is plausible but unconfirmed by neutral tests — treat the marketing numbers with caution until third-party scores land.
briefs.NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra:
NVIDIA's open-weights frontier model, announced at Computex June 1 2026 and released June 4. It's a 550B-total / 55B-active hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE with a 1M-token context, and NVIDIA released the whole stack — weights, reward models, quantized variants, and training recipes — under its Open Model License. AA Index: 48.

Its standout traits are speed and openness: it's the fastest US open-weights frontier model (>300 tokens/second) and the best US open-weight on intelligence (AA 48), with an unusually complete open release. The honest limitation is the global standing — that 48 still trails the leading Chinese open models (Kimi K2.6 sat at 54), so it leads its national/regional bracket more than the open field overall, and it's text-only.
briefs.MAI-Thinking-1:
Microsoft AI's first in-house reasoning model, unveiled at Build 2026 (released June 2). It's a ~1T-total / 35B-active sparse MoE with a 256K context, built for reasoning. The strategically notable part: Microsoft trained it explicitly WITHOUT OpenAI data — a deliberate decoupling from its longtime partner. It posts very strong math: AIME 2025 97, AIME 2026 94.5.

Strengths are reasoning and math, where it's competitive with Anthropic's Opus 4.6 on SWE-bench Pro and was preferred over Claude Sonnet 4.6 in a blind human evaluation (Surge). The caveats: it's closed-weights with no public price listed here, and the headline story is as much about Microsoft proving independence from OpenAI as about a clear capability lead — it's competitive with, not dominant over, the frontier cluster.
briefs.MAI-Code-1-Flash:
Microsoft AI's in-house coding model, part of a seven-model MAI drop at Build 2026 (released June 2). It's positioned as a fast, efficient coding specialist and posts SWE-bench Pro 51.2.

Its strength is efficiency-per-capability in the small/fast coding tier: it beats Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5 on all four core coding benchmarks, including a 16-point SWE-bench Pro lead (51.2 vs 35.2), and solves harder tasks with up to 60% fewer tokens. The limits are scope and disclosure — it's a narrow coding model (not a general reasoner), closed-weights with no listed price, and its 51.2 SWE-bench Pro, while strong for its class, sits below the top flagships (Opus 4.8 at 69.2). Its params and context aren't disclosed here.
briefs.Meta Muse Spark:
Released April 8 2026, this is Meta's FIRST proprietary, closed-weight model — a sharp break from the open Llama line that defined the company (Meta says it 'hopes to open-source future versions'). Built by its Superintelligence Labs, it's natively multimodal (voice/text/image in, text out) and free to use at meta.ai. AA Index: 52.

Its strengths skew toward health and hard reasoning: it leads its peers on HealthBench Hard (42.8) and on HLE-Contemplating (HLE 50.2), and it matches Llama 4 Maverick with over 10x less compute — an efficiency win. The weaknesses are coding and agentic tasks, where it trails, and the strategic cost of going closed. At AA Index 52 it's a capable mid-frontier model rather than the outright best, but the health-benchmark strength makes it worth noting for a medical audience.
briefs.GLM-5:
From Chinese lab Zhipu / Z.ai, released February 11 2026. It's a ~745B-total / 44B-active MoE (256 experts, 8 active) flagship, open-weight under the permissive MIT license, with a 200K context and an agentic focus. At launch it held the top open-weights AA Index score (50) and rivaled OpenAI's GPT-5.2. Benchmarks: SWE-bench 77.8, HLE 50.4 — that HLE figure actually beat Claude Opus 4.5.

Its strength is being a genuinely frontier-competitive model you can download and run freely (MIT), with a notable Humanity's Last Exam result. The caveats are the usual open-weights ceiling — AA Index 50 leads the open pack but sits below the closed frontier (mid-50s to 60s) — plus it's text-only, and it was quickly iterated (GLM-5.1 on March 27, then the stronger GLM-5.2), so this exact version was a fast-moving snapshot.
briefs.GLM-5.2:
Zhipu / Z.ai's June 13 2026 open-weight (MIT) refresh, and a strong value-frontier model. It's a ~744B-total / ~40B-active MoE with a 1M-token context, and it introduced 'IndexShare' attention that cuts per-token compute 2.9x at full 1M context. Benchmarks: SWE-bench Pro 62.1, HLE 54.7, Terminal-Bench 2.1 82.7, AIME 99.2.

The headline strength is cost: it beat OpenAI's GPT-5.5 on several long-horizon coding benchmarks at roughly 1/6 the cost, and it leads on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (best-harness) and agentic math (AIME 99.2) — all with freely available weights. The honest limit is raw coding: its 62.1 SWE-bench Pro trails Claude Opus 4.8 (69.2). So it's arguably the best open-weight value of its moment, just not the single strongest model on every axis.
briefs.DeepSeek-V4-Pro:
DeepSeek-V4-Pro is the Chinese lab's April 2026 return to the open frontier — a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with just 49B parameters active per token and a 1-million-token default context. Its headline is efficiency: a new hybrid attention design (Compressed Sparse plus Heavily Compressed Attention) cuts per-token compute to roughly a quarter of the prior V3.2 and KV-cache memory to about a tenth at full context, so a frontier-class open model runs unusually cheaply at long context. The weights are public.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 52 (live v4.0 scale), making it the #2 open-weights model behind Moonshot's Kimi K2.6 and ahead of GLM-5 and NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra. It is strongest on math, STEM and coding, where DeepSeek says it leads all current open models, and on world knowledge. The limits: it shipped as a preview with no stable GA, it trails the closed frontier (Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro) on the overall index, and as a text-only model it skips the native multimodality that rivals like Qwen3.5 now offer.
briefs.DeepSeek-V4-Flash:
DeepSeek-V4-Flash is the smaller, faster half of the April 2026 V4 launch — a 284-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with about 13B active per token, sharing V4-Pro's 1-million-token default context and the same compressed-attention machinery for cheap long-context inference. It targets high-volume, latency-sensitive workloads where V4-Pro's full scale is overkill, and like its sibling it ships with open weights under a preview label.

The trade-off is the usual one for a Flash-class model: it gives up raw intelligence and hard-reasoning depth for throughput and cost, so it sits well below the frontier on composite benchmarks and is best read as DeepSeek's answer to Gemini 3 Flash and the small Qwen models rather than a competitor to the flagship tier. DeepSeek has not published independent frontier-benchmark numbers for it, so its exact standing is still soft.
briefs.Seed 2.1 Pro:
Seed 2.1 Pro is ByteDance's coding-focused flagship from its Seed research team, unveiled at the Volcano Engine 2026 conference on June 23 as an early-access preview rather than a finished production model. It is the company's first entry to register on cross-lab leaderboards, debuting #8 on the Code Arena: Frontend track with a 1539 Elo — roughly level with Claude Opus 4.6 — and placing top-10 in five of seven subcategories, including React and brand/marketing builds.

Its clear strength is web-frontend generation and editing, where it was specifically tuned over the earlier general-purpose Seed 2.0 Pro. The limits are mostly unknowns: ByteDance has disclosed no parameter count, context window, pricing, or whether the weights will be open, and the public rank reflects a preview build, so general reasoning, agentic, and multi-language coding strength outside the frontend niche remain unproven.
briefs.GPT-5.6 Sol:
GPT-5.6 is OpenAI's mid-2026 flagship suite, shipped in three tiers — Sol (strongest, $5/$30), Terra (balanced, $2.50/$15) and Luna (fast/cheap, $1/$6). It debuted June 26 not as a normal launch but as a government-gated preview restricted to ~20 U.S.-vetted partner organizations, the same access-review regime that had frozen Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5. On July 8 the Commerce Department (CAISI) lifted the hold after security testing, and OpenAI confirmed broad public availability across API, ChatGPT and Codex starting July 9 — the first frontier model to be gov-gated pre-release and then cleared.

Sol's reported strengths are coding, biology and cybersecurity — it is OpenAI's most capable cyber model to date, with strong ExploitGym gains, and posts HealthBench Professional 60.5. Terra is pitched as roughly GPT-5.5-level performance at half the cost, and Sol is served on Cerebras at up to 750 tokens/second. The main caveat is timing risk: as of this sweep it is cleared and dated but not yet in general hands, and independent AA-Index placement against Fable 5 (60) and Opus 4.8 (56) won't be settled until it's broadly benchmarked post-launch.
briefs.Claude Sonnet 5:
Claude Sonnet 5 is Anthropic's mid-tier model, launched Jun 30 2026 as the default for Free and Pro users and the same day Fable 5 and Mythos 5 came back from their export-control freeze. It's the most agentic Sonnet yet — built to plan, run terminals and drive browsers on its own — and its first independent Artificial Analysis score (53 on the v4.1 Intelligence Index, #5 overall) lands it just 2-3 points behind GPT-5.5 and Anthropic's own flagship Opus 4.8.

Its strength is agentic coding value: SWE-bench Pro 63.2% and Terminal-Bench 2.1 80.4% put it within reach of Opus 4.8's coding at a fraction of the price, and it actually edges Opus 4.8 on the GDPval-AA and AA-Briefcase agentic evals. The trade-offs are deliberate — it was not trained on offensive-cyber tasks (0% on Firefox exploit development by design) and ships with cyber safeguards on, and a retuned tokenizer counts ~1.0-1.35x more tokens per task, so its real cost per task runs higher than the $2/$10 intro sticker suggests.
briefs.LongCat-2.0:
LongCat-2.0 is Meituan's 1.6-trillion-parameter open-weight coding model, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts system that activates only about 48 billion parameters per token and carries a native 1-million-token context under an MIT license. Its headline isn't just the size: Meituan says it trained the whole thing end-to-end on roughly 50,000 domestic Chinese ASICs, none of them US-export-restricted, and unmasked it as 'Owl Alpha,' the stealth model that had been topping OpenRouter for two months.

It is strongest at agentic software engineering, where its 59.5 on SWE-bench Pro nudges past GPT-5.5 and it posts 70.8 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 77.3 on SWE-bench Multilingual. The main caveats are practical rather than technical: at announcement the actual weights were still 'coming soon' on GitHub and Hugging Face, so it's open-in-intent but not yet downloadable, and its published numbers lean on coding and long-horizon agentic tasks rather than a full independent frontier-intelligence sweep.
briefs.Gemini 3.5 Flash:
Gemini 3.5 Flash is Google DeepMind's mid-2026 fast-and-cheap tier, announced May 19 and now generally available across the Gemini app, Google AI Studio and the Gemini API. It's natively multimodal (text, image, audio and video in), carries a 1M-token context window, and is priced at $1.50/$9.00 per million tokens. The headline is that it beats the larger Gemini 3.1 Pro on several agentic and coding benchmarks while running roughly three times faster.

It's strongest at high-throughput agentic coding and tool-use — 76.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 55.1% on SWE-bench Pro — plus vision and spatial reasoning, all at Flash-tier speed and cost. The trade-off is that it isn't a true frontier flagship: on the hardest reasoning it still trails top-end models like Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, and Google positions it for scale and latency rather than peak intelligence.
